sentences.text: Tenontosaurus was an iguanodontian ornithopod dinosaur featuring a thick, U-shaped beak formed by flaring premaxillae. The vomer bone extended from the beak to the back of the eye socket, making it the longest in the skull. Its lower jaw ended in a predentary bone, a structure unique to ornithischians that formed the lower beak.
This animal possessed an unusually long and broad tail that was stiffened by a network of bony tendons, similar to its back.

The first fossil was discovered in Big Horn County, Montana, by an AMNH expedition in 1903. Barnum Brown informally named the animal 'Tenantosaurus' or 'sinew lizard' due to its stiffening tendons. John Ostrom scientifically described the taxon as Tenontosaurus tilletti in 1970 based on fossils from the Cloverly Formation. The species name 'tilletti' honors the Lloyd Tillett family, who assisted Yale field parties.

Gregory S. Paul estimated that T. dossi was 7 meters long and weighed 1000 kg. Tenontosaurus was a facultative quadruped capable of standing on either two or four legs. It likely used a quadrupedal stance for feeding but was probably unable to move rapidly on four legs. Adult Tenontosaurus could browse vegetation up to a height of about 3 meters when standing on two legs.

The genus Tenontosaurus was described by John Ostrom in 1970 and contains two species: the type species T. tilletti and T. dossi described by Winkler, Murry, and Jacobs in 1997. Tenontosaurus was originally placed in the family Iguanodontidae but later reclassified into Hypsilophodontidae.

Tenontosaurus lived during the mid-Cretaceous period, between approximately 122 and 108 million years ago, from the Aptian to the Albian stages. The time range for Tenontosaurus is recorded as the Aptian to Cenomanian, spanning from 121.4 to 93.9 million years ago. When Tenontosaurus first appeared in Wyoming and Montana during the early Albian age, the climate was arid to semi-arid with seasonal rainfall and occasional droughts. It lived in a paleoenvironment of tropical or sub-tropical forests, floodplains, and swamps similar to modern-day Louisiana.

It is debated whether Ostrom's original reconstruction of the Tenontosaurus skull accurately represented its true depth, as it may have been exaggerated. Scientists debate Tenontosaurus's exact phylogenetic position, with some studies linking it closer to dryomorphs and others placing it as a sister taxon to a clade of rhabdodontids and dryomorphs. It is debated whether Tenontosaurus dossi represents a direct ancestor with teeth to Tenontosaurus tilletti, as it is unlikely to be the ancestor of the rest of the group, suggesting the toothless trait may have evolved separately.
